title: testing/synctest: deterministic time for concurrent tests
summary: synctest.Test runs a test in a bubble with a fake clock that jumps forward whenever every goroutine in it is blocked. Timeouts, backoff and heartbeats are tested instantly and exactly, with no clock interface in the production code.

examples.title: Seven seconds of backoff in zero real time

annotations.note: Ordinary production code: time.After and a context deadline, nothing test-specific. synctest swaps the clock underneath, so there is no Clock interface to inject.
synctest.Test (Go 1.25) runs the function in a bubble. Goroutines started inside belong to it, and the time package inside uses a fake clock that starts at midnight UTC on 2000-01-01.
retry waits 1s, 2s and 4s. Whenever every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, the clock jumps to the next timer, so seven seconds of waiting take no real time: the PASS line shows (0.00s).
Fake time is exact, so the test asserts equality. With real time it could only check "at least 7s, not much more", and every run would cost seven seconds.
Deadlines are timers too. The context fires at exactly 5s, in the middle of the 4s wait that would have ended at 7s, and retry returns the cause.

examples.title: Checking state just before and after a timeout with synctest.Sleep

annotations.note: The goroutine under test. Its timer belongs to the bubble's clock. Since Go 1.23, Reset on an unfired timer needs no Stop-and-drain dance: no stale value can arrive afterwards.

When the test function returns, t.Context() is canceled and the goroutine exits. synctest.Test waits for every goroutine in the bubble, and fails the test if they are deadlocked, so a leaked goroutine can't go unnoticed.
Beat is an unbuffered send to the watchdog goroutine. The clock can't move until that goroutine is blocked again, so its Reset happens at exactly 20s.
synctest.Sleep (Go 1.27) is time.Sleep followed by synctest.Wait: the clock moves, then every other goroutine in the bubble runs until it blocks. On Go 1.25 and 1.26, write those two calls.

At 50s the test's sleep and the watchdog's timer fire at the same fake instant. After a plain time.Sleep, which goroutine runs first is unpredictable and the check could see dead == false; the Wait inside synctest.Sleep lets the watchdog finish its turn first.

use_cases: Retry and backoff: assert the exact schedule (1s, 2s, 4s) without waiting seven seconds
Timeouts, TTL caches, heartbeats and debouncers: check the state just before and just after the boundary
Code built on context.WithTimeout, time.AfterFunc or tickers whose tests used to need long sleeps or an injected clock
HTTP timeouts over an in-memory network: net.Pipe, or httptest.NewTestServer (Go 1.27)
strengths: No clock abstraction in production code: it keeps calling time.Now and time.After, where Java tests typically need a java.time.Clock passed in
Time advances by itself when everything is blocked, unlike Vitest or Jest fake timers, where the test calls advanceTimersByTime(ms) and has to know how far
Assertions are exact (got == 7*time.Second), with no tolerance windows and no flaky sleeps on a loaded CI machine
A bubble whose goroutines end up deadlocked fails the test instead of hanging until the go test timeout
weaknesses: Only blocking inside the bubble counts. Real network I/O, system calls and mutex waits aren't durably blocking, so code under test needs in-memory fakes such as net.Pipe
Go 1.25 or later (synctest.Sleep: 1.27); projects stuck on older toolchains still need an injected clock
Bubble rules take some learning: no t.Run or t.Parallel inside, and channels and timers created in a bubble panic when used from outside

pitfalls.title: Real network I/O inside the bubble
pitfalls.detail: A goroutine reading from a TCP socket isn't durably blocked, so the clock won't advance past it and Wait keeps waiting. Use net.Pipe or httptest.NewTestServer, whose in-memory network works with synctest.

pitfalls.title: Channels created outside the bubble
pitfalls.detail: Only operations on channels created inside the bubble count as durably blocking. Create the system under test inside the synctest.Test function, not in a package variable or TestMain.

pitfalls.title: time.Sleep when another goroutine wakes at the same instant
pitfalls.detail: Two goroutines woken at the same fake time run in unpredictable order. Follow the sleep with synctest.Wait, or use synctest.Sleep (Go 1.27).

pitfalls.title: Copying examples written for the Go 1.24 experiment
pitfalls.detail: Go 1.24 had synctest.Run behind GOEXPERIMENT=synctest. Go 1.25 replaced it with synctest.Test(t, f); Run is not in the Go 1.27 package.

quiz.q: When does the fake clock inside a synctest bubble advance?
options: When every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked
Only when the test calls synctest.Wait
quiz.why: The clock jumps to the next pending timer once nothing in the bubble can make progress without time passing.

quiz.q: Which of these does not count as durably blocking?
options: Receiving from a channel created in the bubble
sync.WaitGroup.Wait after Add was called in the bubble
quiz.why: A mutex can be released by a goroutine outside the bubble, so a goroutine waiting on one is not durably blocked.

options: Sleeps for d of real time
Moves the clock by d without blocking
quiz.why: Its docs define it as exactly those two calls: advance the fake clock, then let the other goroutines settle.

body:
## Concept

Testing concurrent code with timeouts used to mean one of two compromises: real sleeps
(slow and flaky) or a clock interface threaded through production code.
`testing/synctest` (Go 1.25) removes both.

`synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ... })` runs the function in a **bubble**. Every
goroutine started inside belongs to the bubble, and inside it the `time` package runs on
a **fake clock** that starts at midnight UTC, 2000-01-01. The clock only moves when
every goroutine in the bubble is **durably blocked**, meaning only another goroutine in
the same bubble could wake it. Then it jumps straight to the next timer.

Two helpers control the timing inside a test:

- `synctest.Wait()` blocks until every other goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked,
  so you can assert on state once the system has settled.
- `synctest.Sleep(d)` (Go 1.27) is `time.Sleep(d)` followed by `synctest.Wait()`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS**: Vitest's `vi.useFakeTimers()` and Jest's fake timers replace `setTimeout`,
  but the test drives them with `advanceTimersByTime(ms)`. In a bubble the clock
  advances on its own whenever nothing else can happen, across all goroutines.
- **Java**: the usual approach is injecting a `java.time.Clock` or a fake
  `ScheduledExecutorService`, plus Awaitility-style polling. synctest needs neither:
  production code keeps calling `time.Now` and `time.After`.
- **Python**: `freezegun` or `time-machine` freeze `time.time()`, but a thread that is
  sleeping still sleeps in real time. The bubble controls sleeps, timers and deadlines
  together.
- **C++**: comparable to templating code on a clock type, done by the runtime instead.

## How it works

The runtime tracks every goroutine in the bubble. A goroutine is durably blocked when it
is blocked on a send, receive or `select` over channels created in the bubble, on
`time.Sleep`, on `sync.Cond.Wait`, or on `sync.WaitGroup.Wait` when `Add` was called in
the bubble. Locking a `sync.Mutex`, network I/O and system calls are not durably
blocking, because something outside the bubble could end them.

When every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked:

1. if the test is in `synctest.Wait`, `Wait` returns;
2. otherwise, while the test function is still running, the clock jumps to the next
   time that would wake a goroutine;
3. if there is no such time, the bubble is deadlocked: `synctest.Test` panics and the
   test fails.

`synctest.Test` returns only after every goroutine in the bubble has exited. Inside the
bubble, `t.Context()` has a `Done` channel that belongs to the bubble, and `t.Run`,
`t.Parallel` and `t.Deadline` must not be called.

These examples run with `go test -v`. Real time per test is milliseconds, while the
logged fake time is seconds.

## Design notes

Write production code against the real `time` and `context` APIs, and let tests decide
how time passes. Reserve injected clocks for the cases synctest doesn't cover, such as
code that has to block on real I/O.

A useful test shape: start the system inside the bubble, `synctest.Sleep` to just
before the interesting moment and assert nothing has happened yet, then to just after
and assert that it did. `synctest.Wait()` on its own is the way to assert "this has
not happened": once it returns, nothing else can happen without time moving.

Fake networks keep tests inside the bubble: `net.Pipe` for raw connections, and
`httptest.NewTestServer` (Go 1.27), whose in-memory network suits synctest, for HTTP.
